title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: An Introduction to the APJR
keywords: Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary
Executive Committee for the Judicial Reform Program
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's introduction to the 156-page 'Action Program for Judicial Reform 2001-2006' (APJR), the implementing effort envisioned in Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.'s 'Davide Watch,' followed by the verbatim reprint of the program's Executive Summary

The provenance and governance of the APJR: it takes its bearing from the earlier 'Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary' and from nationwide stakeholder consultations held under Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa and funded by a UNDP grant; approved by the Supreme Court on December 8, 2000 and superintended by an Executive Committee chaired by the Chief Justice himself

The reform framework reprinted from the Executive Summary: nine fundamental principles, a four-pronged sectoral program (judicial systems and procedures, institutions development, human resource development, reform support systems), and seven critical issues that cut across all sectors

The investment and management plan: PhP 4.3 billion for 2001-2006, 53.45% domestic and 46.55% external, allocated 75.47% to institutions development, 18.33% to human resources, 5.83% to systems and procedures and the remainder to reform support -- with phasing, sequencing, monitoring and a program management office to run it
sub_topics: He identifies the 'Davide Watch,' announced immediately after Davide assumed office on November 30, 1998, as the centerpiece of the Chief Justice's stewardship, and notes he had already written about it extensively in his book 'Leadership by Example'
He states the present volume's narrower focus: the implementing effort, detailed in the 156-page 'Action Program for Judicial Reform 2001-2006'

He describes the APJR as 'comprehensive, pervasive and wide-ranging,' built on past reform initiatives and on consultations with stakeholders across the country held under CJ Narvasa and funded by the UNDP

He records the approval date -- December 8, 2000 -- and names the full Executive Committee for the Judicial Reform Program, from Davide as chairman and Bellosillo as vice chairman through Puno, Panganiban, Melencio Herrera, Velasco, Villarama, Dujua, Khan, Soriano, Uy, Dumdum, Department of Justice Assistant Secretary Atanacio and Integrated Bar of the Philippines National President Pilando, plus the technical staff

He underlines the APJR's standing: it is 'the only standing committee in the Supreme Court that is directly headed by the Chief Justice,' with a full-time Program Management Office under Evelyn Toledo-Dumdum handling day-to-day implementation
He explains that the full text is too long to reprint and that he is instead reproducing the Executive Summary verbatim as background for the whole book
The Executive Summary opens by conceding that past efforts to address judicial problems, 'though numerous, have been sporadic,' and presents the APJR as the first long-term foundation

It restates the Davide Watch vision -- a judiciary 'independent, effective and efficient, and worthy of public trust and confidence' and a legal profession offering 'quality ethical, accessible and cost-effective legal services' -- and six mission goals from speedy justice to dignity, integrity, accountability and transparency

It lists the earlier studies the APJR builds on, including the Justice and Development Project that produced the 'Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary' and reviews of the criminal justice system, alternative dispute resolution and the barangay justice system

Section 1 sets out nine guiding principles, from impartiality and access through judicial autonomy, decentralization, information-systems-based operations, competitive remuneration, transparency in appointments, and collaboration with civil society

It names the seven critical issues: case congestion and delay, budget deficiencies, a politicized appointments system, lack of judicial autonomy, re-engineering of human resource development, dysfunctional administrative structures and deficient court technology, and the need for better public information and civil-society collaboration

Section 2 gives the money: PhP 4.3 billion total, PhP 2.305 billion domestic and PhP 2.007 billion from official development assistance, with capital outlays at 28.31% and PhP 786 million for studies and re-engineering projects

It breaks the investment down by sector -- PhP 3.2 billion for institutions development (fiscal autonomy, administrative re-engineering, information systems, infrastructure), PhP 791 million for human resources (appointments, training, judicial education, remuneration, legal education), PhP 251 million for judicial systems and procedures (ADR, barangay justice, performance management, judicial research group), and about PhP 16 million for reform support systems (public information, civil society, international best practice)
It anticipates external financing peaking in 2001-2002 for assessment and project preparation and then declining, with reliance on domestic funding during implementation to ensure sustainability

Section 3 sets out program management: phasing that balances short-term impact against strategic approaches, sequencing that asks which reforms can start independently, which feed later reforms and which are antecedent, and monitoring whose results feed back into planning

It closes by describing the institutional machinery -- an inter-agency steering committee for policy direction, an institutionalized program management or change management unit, and core groups inside implementing offices -- and by calling the APJR 'an evolving document'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' is Artemio V. Panganiban's short introduction to the Action Program for Judicial Reform, followed by the verbatim reprint of that program's Executive Summary. He began by naming the 'Davide Watch' -- announced by Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. immediately after he assumed office on November 30, 1998 -- as the centerpiece of Davide's stewardship, noting that he had already written extensively about that vision in his earlier book 'Leadership by Example' and that this volume would instead focus on 'the implementing effort,' detailed in the 156-page 'Action Program for Judicial Reform 2001-2006.' He described the APJR as 'comprehensive, pervasive and wide-ranging,' taking its bearing from past initiatives, especially the 'Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary,' and from consultations with stakeholders across the country held during Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa's term and funded by a United Nations Development Program grant. Approved by the Supreme Court on December 8, 2000, the program is superintended by an Executive Committee whose full membership he lists, from Davide as chairman and Justice Josue N. Bellosillo as vice chairman through Justices Puno and Panganiban, Philja Chancellor Melencio Herrera, Court Administrator Velasco and the Integrated Bar of the Philippines president, with a technical staff named as well. He stressed that the APJR is 'the only standing committee in the Supreme Court that is directly headed by the Chief Justice,' with a full-time Program Management Office under Evelyn Toledo-Dumdum handling implementation, and, unable to reproduce the full text, reprinted the Executive Summary as background for the book. That summary concedes that earlier efforts, 'though numerous, have been sporadic'; restates the Davide Watch vision of a judiciary 'independent, effective and efficient, and worthy of public trust and confidence' and its six mission goals; sets out nine guiding principles and a four-pronged sectoral program addressing seven critical issues, from case congestion and budget deficiencies to politicized appointments and deficient court technology; costs the 2001-2006 program at PhP 4.3 billion, 53.45 percent domestic and 46.55 percent from official development assistance, with 75.47 percent going to institutions development, 18.33 percent to human resources, 5.83 percent to judicial systems and procedures and about PhP 16 million to reform support systems; anticipates external financing peaking early and declining as domestic funding sustains implementation; and describes the management arrangements -- phasing, sequencing, monitoring and evaluation, an inter-agency steering committee and an institutionalized program management office -- while calling the APJR 'an evolving document' that must remain responsive to the judiciary's and the country's needs.
